title: Peter Village enclosure (15Fa166)
summary: Peter Village, an early earthwork north of Lexington, was first used around 300–200 BCE, likely as a place to gather and work local galena.
bodyMarkdown:
North of Lexington, in the Elkhorn Creek country of Fayette County, lies one of the oldest earthworks in the Bluegrass. Peter Village (site 15Fa166) belongs to the [Mount Horeb Earthworks Complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Horeb_Earthworks_Complex), a group of enclosures and mounds built by the region's early Woodland peoples. Its builders left no written name for the place, and the label "village" was given much later by outside observers.

The earliest use of the site dates to about 300 to 200 BCE. At first it had an earthen enclosure and a wooden palisade; later its builders dug a ditch about two meters deep. Archaeologists consider this early phase pre-Adena and tie it to harvesting and processing [galena](https://grokipedia.com/page/Galena), a lead ore that occurs naturally nearby.

That makes Peter Village less a home than a work and gathering place.

Nineteenth-century observers were the first to record the earthwork in writing. The naturalist [Constantine Samuel Rafinesque](https://grokipedia.com/page/Constantine_Samuel_Rafinesque) described it as a twenty-sided polygon about 3,767 feet around. A ditch some 15 feet wide and 4 to 8 feet deep surrounded it, and the entrance faced south.

Ephraim Squier and Edwin Davis published plans of Peter Village and nearby Grimes Village in their 1848 survey, *Ancient Monuments of the Mississippi Valley*. Their engraving remains one of the best records of the earthwork's shape. Much of that shape has since been worn down by plowing and development.

Peter Village sits within the same complex as the Mount Horeb ceremonial circle, [told separately here](/stories/mount-horeb-earthworks/). Together they show that people of the [Adena culture](https://grokipedia.com/page/Adena_culture) and their predecessors shaped the Bluegrass into a landscape of gathering places many centuries before Kentucky's forts and stations. Adena is an archaeologists' name for a shared way of life, not the name of a single tribe.

## Kentucky today

Peter Village is a protected archaeological site, so this site names it but does not map it. Nearby, the University of Kentucky's Adena Park preserves the Mount Horeb earthwork, and the Squier and Davis plan of Peter Village can be viewed online.
